title: How often Exponent shows up in court cases
what: The number of court decisions and federal case files each year where 'Exponent' appears close to expert-witness language (words like expert, testimony, Daubert), plus a normalized rate that corrects for how many cases get digitized in the first place.
how: We searched CourtListener - a free public archive of millions of US court records run by the nonprofit Free Law Project - for Exponent near expert-witness terms, year by year. Because the archive itself grows over time, we divide Exponent's mentions by the TOTAL number of cases in the archive that year: the 'per 100,000 cases' line. A rising normalized line means Exponent's share of litigation is genuinely growing, not just that more cases got scanned.
thesis: Roughly 60% of Exponent's revenue is reactive work - much of it litigation support and expert testimony. If the firm's courtroom footprint is stable or growing relative to all litigation, the core franchise is healthy. This directly tests the 'litigation demand' leg of the thesis.
caveats: Courts only name experts who formally testify; the much larger volume of behind-the-scenes consulting never appears in any public record. This chart sees the tip of the iceberg.
Most product-liability cases happen in STATE courts, which this archive covers thinly - federal cases dominate here.

'Exponent' is also an ordinary English/math word - and CourtListener's word-stemming even matches the Spanish legal word 'exponente'. We removed 421 Spanish-language Puerto Rico false matches; an earlier version of this chart showed a dramatic post-2022 spike that was almost entirely that artifact. What survives the cleaning is the honest picture below.
Written OPINIONS rarely name the testifying firm (a few cases a year) - read that line as 'presence', not market share. The federal CASE-FILE line is the meaningful volume series.

The most recent 1-2 years of the case-file line read artificially LOW: documents only enter this archive when a member of the public buys them from the court system, which lags new filings by months to years.
